tldr: This is a research-theme thread of unrelated arXiv QA papers, not a single event. It opened Nov 12 with SAGE-QA questioning Exact Match scoring on SQuAD 2.0, then JET (Nov 17) targeted tool-calling agents that keep exploring a repository after they already have enough to answer.
whats_new: Two Nov 25 papers turn to QA memory: scene-graph memory repairs lift answerability from 27.2% to 37.4% without reliably improving QA accuracy, and Knowledge-Base Gradient Descent gains on generated questions but is mixed on human ones.
why_it_matters: Across all four papers, the proxy metric (Exact Match, answerability, generated-question scores) diverges from real answer quality, so RAG and agent evals built on those proxies can misreport progress.

beats.headline: SAGE-QA challenges Exact Match scoring for grounded, abstention-aware QA
beats.summary: Scores whether an answer is supported by the passage or correctly abstains on SQuAD 2.0.

beats.headline: JET tunes code-repository QA agents to stop exploring once they have enough
beats.summary: Targets tool-calling agents that keep invoking tools after gathering sufficient evidence.

beats.headline: Memory structures for QA: better structure scores do not always mean better answers
beats.summary: Scene-graph memory and self-editing knowledge bases both show gains on internal metrics that do not fully carry to QA accuracy or human questions.

open_questions: How far do SQuAD 2.0 model rankings move when scored with SAGE-QA instead of Exact Match?
Is SAGE-QA's grounding check released as code that can be dropped into an existing RAG eval harness?
Does JET's early-stopping cut tool calls on repositories outside its training benchmark without lowering answer accuracy?
Does Knowledge-Base Gradient Descent improve results on human-written questions in any follow-up evaluation?
take_for_builders: Before trusting a QA or RAG eval gain, check it against a hand-graded sample of real user questions; treat all four papers as preprints until reproduced.
